# 14. Art and audio

A roguelike shows the same few glyphs, tiles, sounds and loops thousands of times across its runs. That makes presentation a budget and a language before it is decoration: whatever you make has to be cheap enough to produce in the quantity a roguelike needs, quick to read in a dangerous moment, and slow to wear out by the two-hundredth run. The first half of this chapter is about what the player sees: the choice between characters and pictures, what abstraction does for the player, the craft of text art, tiles and creature design, how small teams get art they can afford, and how to make generated spaces look art-directed. The second half is about motion and sound: juice, sound design, music written for repetition, generative music, and music tied to the world rather than to a timeline. It ends with experiments that treat the display itself as unexplored territory.

Most of the talks come from practitioners: artists who drew tilesets and ASCII scenes, composers who scored roguelikes, and solo developers who had to do all of it themselves. So much of the chapter is technique specific enough to copy. The recurring argument is that abstraction is a strength, because it lets players imagine and lets designers afford a large cast. Where a game moves beyond it, the talks ask for one coherent style, effects that fit the tone, and sound designed for repetition and for an order of play nobody can predict.

## In brief

- Character display makes content cheap: a new monster costs a glyph, a colour, a description and its data, which is what lets a roguelike afford a huge cast and complex interactions ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 15:24](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=924); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=485); [Josh Ge 2018, 17:05](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1025)).
- Choosing graphics is choosing an audience: mainstream players expect them, mediocre or half-measure graphics please no one, and the real cost can take most of a project's life ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 16:42](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1002); [Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 31:49](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1909)).
- Low-fidelity representation invites players to imagine and co-create the world, but imagination needs a small trigger of detail rather than switching on by itself ([droqen 2020, 9:01](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=541); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 17:12](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1032); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364)).
- If you offer tiles, make them read like glyphs: a few strong forms and a distinct silhouette, so experienced players recognise each one almost as a symbol ([Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442); [Josh Ge 2016, 23:54](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1434); [Joel Ryan 2022, 15:08](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=908)).
- Design a creature's look backwards from its mechanics, so the art tells players what it does before they have to learn its name ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1576); [Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 7:34](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=454)).
- On a small budget, kitbash new assets from a small set of compatible parts, and guard coherence above all, because mixing sources with different styles is what makes cheap art look cheap ([Sergio Garces 2022, 2:04](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=124); [Max Bottega 2024, 5:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=308); [Phillip Daigle 2020, 15:20](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=920); [Sergio Garces 2022, 6:30](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=390); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 5:16](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=316); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048)).
- Juice is coded, not drawn: tweens of scale, position, rotation and colour make turns feel alive and are within a solo programmer's reach, as long as they fit the game's tone ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 9:22](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=562); [Chris McCormick 2021, 3:56](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=236); [Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:00](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1620); [Tabea Iseli 2022, 10:34](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=634)).
- Sound suits abstract games: it supports the player's imagination without hijacking it, and roguelike developers' feel for symbols carries straight over to it ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 1:12](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=72); [Josh Ge 2016, 17:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1034)).
- Write music for repetition: segmented loops, pacing to play and crossfaded variants fight ear fatigue, and changes of music can mark the player's progress through a run or a level ([Crashtroid 2023, 2:56](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=176); [Crashtroid 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=226); [Crashtroid 2023, 13:43](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=823); [Jon Perry 2025, 12:19](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=739); [Nifflas 2025, 27:47](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=1667)).
- Do not plan on splicing recorded voice for non-linear content: two independent talks warn that it does not survive being chopped up and rearranged ([Paul Dean 2025, 26:19](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1579); [Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 12:51](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=771)).

## ASCII or graphics: what the choice costs and buys

The first presentation decision in a roguelike is whether to draw the world in characters or in pictures, and the talks treat it as a decision about cost and audience more than taste.

### What characters buy you

Two speakers, in separate talks, put the case for characters in almost the same terms: they make content cheap. Santiago Zapata calls character-based display perhaps Rogue's second most important legacy after procedural generation, and explains why: a new monster needs a glyph, a colour, a description and its data, and nothing more. There is no sprite to draw, no model and no animation for each way it can interact with other things. Because interactions only have to be described, not animated, they can be very complex; doing the same with full graphics is very expensive ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 15:24](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=924)). Evan Ovadia makes the same comparison: a sprite might need 20 poses, while a character needs a letter and a colour and fits the game's style automatically, so you can add a creature in moments and spend the time on gameplay and story ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=485)). Ovadia adds reusability: any letter works with any foreground and background colour, so a green `o` is an orc and a purple `o` its chieftain, where a goblin sprite is hard to recolour into anything else ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:30](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=510)). Josh Ge, recommending asset choices for a new roguelike, says the same thing more briefly: ASCII makes it easy to add new content, and with good foreground and background colour combinations it can look beautiful, as the range of styles in games like Brogue shows ([Josh Ge 2018, 17:05](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1025)).

> Design efficiency is super important for roguelikes. — [Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=485)

The saving is not only in production hours. JP LeBreton chose ASCII for their roguelite partly because it was within their abilities as an artist: a finite, visible set of characters and colours reduces and discretises the decisions you face on a blank page, which makes it easier to start drawing. It also gives you the advantages of tile-based level editing; LeBreton's tool Playscii was used to lay out the Frog Fractions 2 overworld map ([JP LeBreton 2019, 6:11](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=371)). And abstraction makes simulation cheap to show. Rich Wilson points out that in Dwarf Fortress, depicting someone sitting in a chair means drawing two glyphs on top of each other, whereas at AAA fidelity the same act involves capsule collision, nav meshes and animation problems; Wilson notes that many immersive sims are set on abandoned space stations precisely because NPCs are hard ([Rich Wilson 2021, 25:13](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1513)).

Coloured characters are not a new idea. Jeff Olson recalls that Alphaman used coloured ASCII when most roguelikes were monochrome; Olson admits it does not look like much today but says that next to the "prison grey" of its contemporaries it was striking ([Jeff Olson 2023, 2:07](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=127)).

### What graphics buy you, and what they cost

The counter-argument is about who you want to reach. Zapata, whose game Hope was their first graphical one and was made without a good pixel artist, says that moving to graphics targets a much larger audience with different expectations: console-mode players fill gaps with imagination, graphics players expect clear feedback and polish, so mediocre graphics please no one ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949)). Thomas Biskup reaches the same conclusion from the commercial side. Ultimate ADOM made a good graphical version its prime focus because ASCII alone does not enlarge the audience, keeping ASCII mainly for fast prototyping ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 34:03](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=2043)), and two years later Biskup put it bluntly: for the mainstream you need graphics, because mainstream users do not really get ASCII ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 16:42](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1002)). Neither speaker disparages ASCII; both say the choice follows from the audience you are aiming at.

Budget for the real cost before you commit. Biskup reports that ADOM's team underestimated the effort of putting a graphical interface on an ASCII game and drawing images for its many items and monsters: it took three and a half to four of the project's five years, even with a graphics library that helped immensely. Biskup disagrees with people who say art can be done in a week ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 31:49](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1909)). The choice of projection is itself a cost decision. Ultimate ADOM chose 2.5D (3D walls, 2D sprites) after rejecting full 3D as too expensive, plain 2D as too limited, and isometric because it means constantly deciding which walls to fade and makes targeting hard. Biskup also notes that ADOM's barely visible grid made it hard for casual players even to hit a target, so the new version shows the grid clearly ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 11:23](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=683)).

Zapata warns against the obvious compromise. Swapping each character for a static sprite is a half-measure: full graphics for complex interactions is very expensive, and if you do not go all the way players feel it is not enough, so either commit fully or stay with characters. Zapata concedes, though, that modern players want graphics and most of the time you will need them ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977)).

There are other ways to add visual appeal without replacing the glyphs. Josh Ge argues that animated interfaces draw mainstream players without taking anything away from a roguelike, and in Cogmind, where the player is a robot seeing the world through its interfaces, the animation also reinforces the theme ([Josh Ge 2016, 25:57](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1557)).

Sometimes the game's geometry settles the question. Zeno Rogue explains that pixel art fits a non-Euclidean game poorly: pixels are squares, and hyperbolic space has no squares, so HyperRogue uses simple vector-style graphics instead ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 25:33](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1533)).

**In practice:**

- Decide by audience and content volume. If your design depends on a huge cast and complex interactions, characters are what make that affordable ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 15:24](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=924); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=485)). If you need a mainstream audience, plan for graphics ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 34:03](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=2043); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 16:42](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1002)).
- Cost the graphics honestly: every item and monster, every interaction you will have to show, and the interface work around them ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 31:49](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1909)).
- Do not ship a half-measure: either commit to graphics at a standard your audience expects or stay with characters ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977); [Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949)).

## What abstraction does for the player

Abstract display is not only cheaper; several speakers argue it does something for the player that detailed art cannot.

### Leaving room for imagination

droqen describes the `@` as a perfect example of boiling away everything that does not matter: it tells you nothing about what your avatar looks like, only what it can do and does. A `g` might be a goblin, and it does not matter how tall it is. droqen sees low-resolution pixel art working the same way, showing only what is necessary and asking players to learn the game's language ([droqen 2020, 9:01](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=541)). Jamie Brittain reaches a similar conclusion: low graphical fidelity cues players to use their imagination and effectively co-create the look and feel of the space with the designer. A Reddit suggestion to imagine NetHack's halls as a thousand metres high changed how Brittain played, and they note that Caves of Qud now treats its ASCII-style presentation as a deliberate function of play rather than a necessity ([Jamie Brittain 2026, 17:12](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1032)). Rich Wilson, citing Understanding Comics, makes the same link between abstraction and players projecting meaning ([Rich Wilson 2021, 25:13](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1513)).

Evan Ovadia adds a qualification that makes the idea usable. Switching to ASCII is only the first step: imagination does not kick in automatically. Ovadia felt it less in plain random levels than in places with a small touch such as flickering floor colours suggesting flames, just enough extra detail to trigger the mind. An orange letter called an "ambling shambler" produces a different image in every player's head. Yet in their own Incendian Falls, where the symbols deliberately did not depict creatures, Ovadia suspects too much colour and detail kept imagination from starting, and calls the secret an open question ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364)). They also treat their own hybrid style as one local maximum among many ways of combining the strengths of ASCII and sprites, with others still to be found; an audience member suggested audio cues, such as a sound when a creature first appears ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:54](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=534)).

Abstraction also shapes how players relate to their avatar. Alexandra Leonhart observes that in ASCII roguelikes the player's glyph shares a typographic lineage with the monster and item glyphs, a "glyph kinship" between the `@` and everything it meets ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:20:19](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=30019)).

### Borrowed meaning

A retro look brings associations with it, and you can use them on purpose. Cara Esten Hurtle sees the constraints of old software, such as the ASCII aesthetic of Caves of Qud and other roguelikes, as a breeding ground for creativity ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 5:08](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=308)), but argues that retro aesthetics are worth using when the old technology tells a story that could not be told any other way, not for their own sake; Hurtle points to work where the noise and distortion of the old medium become part of the message, as in Game Boy Camera photography ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 15:15](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=915)). G blekkenhorst puts nostalgic design to similar use in the interface game The Archive: they chose an interface era to match when the fiction's volunteer cult began migrating its database, emulated different graphic styles to date artefacts from different periods, and argue that nostalgic design works like marketing, setting players up for a specific experience ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 29:30](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=1770)).

Glyph conventions are borrowed meaning too. Chess has no specified visual form, so Chogue, by Pippin Barr and Jonathan Lessard, uses Unicode chess characters and the CGA palette to evoke Rogue and early computing ([Jonathan Lessard 2018, 26:23](https://youtu.be/l1YEJBKehAY?t=1583)). Dwarf Fortress reuses roguelike conventions as homage: ADOM's quote-mark herbs become its taller grass, a natural extension of grass already built from periods, commas and apostrophes, and the DOS Rogue smiley becomes its dwarves ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 21:03](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=1263)).

### Presentation is part of the design

Joseph Hewitt draws a lesson from stage magic: many great magicians perform tricks that are easy to work out but elevate them through performance, so presentation can matter as much as the mechanism, and programmer-designers should not treat everything as a technical problem ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 14:37](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=877)). Even the box cover tells players what game they are getting. Darren Grey contrasts two pieces of Rogue box art: a burly, blood-splattered warrior, and a sensibly dressed figure on tiptoe reaching from a position of low power for a jewel while green eyes watch from the dark. Grey argues the second better conveys the game, a moment of achievement inside extreme, unknown danger, and that framing like this shapes what players think the game is about ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 12:14](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=734)).

**In practice:** choose a representation for what it lets the player imagine and what it signals, then add only the detail that triggers imagination, such as a flicker of colour, rather than detail that fills the gap for them ([droqen 2020, 9:01](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=541); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364)). If you borrow a retro look, know what story it tells ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 15:15](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=915)).

## The craft of text art

Text art has its own techniques, and the talks give enough of them to work from.

### The medium

JP LeBreton describes the data model underneath all ASCII art: a document is a grid of tiles, and each tile holds a character index into a character set, plus foreground and background colour indices into a palette ([JP LeBreton 2019, 5:07](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=307)). The character set and palette you pick have a massive effect on the result. LeBreton bundled the character sets and palettes of 1980s microcomputers into Playscii and found that each has its own personality, like choosing a font, a tileset and a human language at once ([JP LeBreton 2019, 10:22](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=622)).

Within that grid, Gabriel Santos distinguishes three styles: block art for filled shapes (what automatic video-to-ASCII conversion produces), line art for organic characters and objects, and box drawing for geometric, mechanical subjects and UI, as in Cogmind, a game about robots ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 4:47](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=287)). Santos's art is not strictly traditional ASCII: it uses Unicode symbols where they help, but only ones that keep the established style ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 3:53](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=233)). At a 2016 lightning talk, Gabriel (the Stone Story developer) argued that beyond the data-delivering top-down view of games like NetHack, ASCII art can be developed as an art form in its own right, with games as the medium, and showed their iteration on a boss fight to prove it ([Tariq et al. 2016, 30:11](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=1811)).

### Drawing techniques

Santos's techniques, from their talk on ASCII art and animation:

- **Keep letters and digits out of the art.** The eye goes to alphanumerics first and reads them as text, so use them only on purpose. Symbols such as the inverted exclamation mark (for anti-aliasing) and the centre dot (for balance and negative space) suit line art better ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 8:02](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=482)).
- **Small glyph swaps change the lighting.** In Santos's logo, hyphens left gaps that changed the lighting; a solid box-drawing line made it brighter at the top, darker at the bottom and better centred in the font ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 18:34](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=1114)).
- **Anti-alias steep lines.** Because glyphs are horizontally aligned, near-horizontal lines have many gradations within a cell but angles between 60 and 90 degrees do not, and come out jagged. That is acceptable for rock or spiderweb, not for smooth surfaces; marks like exclamation points and quotes smooth them ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 10:08](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=608)).
- **Make glyph treatments a material language.** The same line angle drawn with different glyph combinations can stand for metal, wood or rock; used consistently, readers internalise the mapping and you can paint a bigger picture with it ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 9:31](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=571)).
- **Separate shapes with negative space.** Where overlapping shapes touch, swap some glyphs for empty cells: the gap makes the foreground part read as on top, adds depth and reads faster. Connecting a robot guardian's arm to its belt would make the arm unreadable. A colour shift, such as shading one object light grey, does the same job ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 14:10](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=850)).
- **Get shadows from the floor.** Santos found by accident, on a patterned temple floor, that characters with blank space below them read as shadows over a textured ground, and now adds shadows to everything and uses dithering borrowed from pixel art for lighting ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 15:39](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=939)).

Once you have memorised the common glyph combinations, text art is fast to iterate: in a live demo Santos swapped three versions of a jack-o-lantern's mouth in moments, and argues that this kind of quick exploration is the point ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 13:07](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=787)).

### Colour and effects on the grid

Jeremiah Reid divides roguelikes into on-grid games, where each cell gets only a character and two colours, and off-grid games that rotate, scale and offset. Reid argues that the on-grid constraint still allows striking, juicy results, as Brogue's water and gas and Cogmind's explosions show ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 5:23](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=323)). The talk's cheapest upgrade for a plain ASCII game is to desaturate the garish default colours and think deliberately about the palette ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 13:55](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=835)).

Cogmind gets smooth particles without breaking the terminal look by running them on a hidden subgrid: each visible cell is logically a 9x9 space, cut like a tic-tac-toe board, where particles move and stack, but each tile is still drawn in a single colour, so the aesthetic holds. The same technique animates the interface, which runs about 200 particle engines at once ([Josh Ge 2016, 25:02](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1502)). Santos goes the other way: their emitter has no particle interaction at all, only velocity and ASCII symbols, with emission points stored as metadata in the art, and can fit two particles in one cell. Santos argues projects should be like that, simple and getting the job done ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 2:28](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=148)).

### Animation

Santos builds animated scenes in layers: a static background, a separate animation for each character, and small details such as a chain or a one-glyph candle flame animated on their own ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 1:05](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=65)). The process is the same as for any animation: references, concepts, a key idle pose, and a test of size and composition in context before hours of animating; skip the test and you redo work or clip the character's head, which happened to Santos ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 16:21](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=981)). For build-up animations, work backwards: they drew a pyramid complete, removed one brick per frame, then played the frames in reverse ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 16:57](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=1017)).

**Rules of thumb:**

- Choose the character set and palette as deliberately as a font and a language ([JP LeBreton 2019, 10:22](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=622)).
- Match the style to the subject: line art for the organic, box drawing for machines and UI ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 4:47](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=287)).
- Keep alphanumerics out of pictures; use gaps and colour to separate shapes ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 8:02](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=482); [Gabriel Santos 2019, 14:10](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=850)).
- Before anything else, fix the palette ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 13:55](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=835)).
- Keep effects simple, and if you need finer motion, simulate it below the grid but draw it on the grid ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 2:28](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=148); [Josh Ge 2016, 25:02](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1502)).
- Test size in context before animating ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 16:21](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=981)).

## Tiles that read like glyphs

If you offer tiles, the goal the tile designers in these talks set themselves is to keep what made ASCII legible.

### Strong forms, not pixel noise

Joel Ryan, who drew the Sil-Q tileset, gives each tile a few strong "major forms", solid areas and lines of colour across chest, head, weapon and legs, so that players who have played enough start to see the forms almost like symbols. Ryan's early tiles, where nearly every pixel differed from its neighbour, looked muddy and blended together ([Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442)). Josh Ge reached a similar design for Cogmind. They argue roguelikes should offer tiles because most players use them (in their data, 66 players used tiles against 18 in ASCII mode), but Cogmind's tiles are monochrome and identifiable by shape, which Ge considers important for keeping the roguelike aesthetic ([Josh Ge 2016, 23:54](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1434)). Two tile designers converging on the same idea, tiles that behave like glyphs, is the main lesson of this section.

> My tiles could have major forms where if you played the game enough you would start to see these forms almost like symbols. — [Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442)

### Ryan's toolkit from Sil-Q

Ryan designed Sil-Q's tiles to sit halfway between tiles and ASCII, studying what glyphs do well and carrying it into the art: the player is a diamond, a spider is shaped like an M. Not every monster could look like its letter, but the habit of borrowing from ASCII stayed with them throughout ([Joel Ryan 2022, 5:45](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=345)). From there the talk adds a set of specific points, which Ryan offers as things to keep in mind rather than decisions others should copy:

- **Silhouettes classify.** Ryan says they usually die by pressing keys too quickly when a new monster appears in a corner of the screen. A strong, unique silhouette lets you classify an unfamiliar monster at a glance: spiny legs mean a poisonous spider, a hulking thick-armed figure a knockback troll ([Joel Ryan 2022, 15:08](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=908)).
- **Size signals threat.** The more pixels a monster uses, the more dangerous players perceive it to be. Ryan's first Crebain filled the tile, overrepresenting a minor monster and barely reading as a bird; the first orc used every vertical pixel, leaving no room for later orcs to be bigger. Reserve size to grow over the game or to mark difficulty spikes ([Joel Ryan 2022, 15:58](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=958)).
- **Contrast detail frequency.** When tiles and background share the same level of detail, they blend. Ryan shows a dragon on a noisy background that stays visible mainly because of its black outline once noise is added to it, and disappears when the outline is removed; flat-colour, low-detail tiles over a finely patterned background stay readable ([Joel Ryan 2022, 22:52](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1372)).
- **Decide tileset-wide conventions on day one.** Ryan had to redraw tiles that filled their space and left no room for the black outline that pulls each tile out from its surroundings; the outline was kept on every side except the bottom ([Joel Ryan 2022, 21:33](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1293)).
- **Use colour to classify abilities.** In Sil-Q blue marks ice, red marks fire-branded attacks, and purple marks draining attacks and groups a set of nebulous horrors ([Joel Ryan 2022, 19:01](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1141)).
- **Accept a shared palette.** Sil-Q crashed on Linux unless the tileset was a 256-colour bitmap, which forced a custom shared colour table. Ryan says this restriction improved the tileset, making it more coherent and making Ryan attend to colours that looked identical side by side but differed by a few values ([Joel Ryan 2022, 11:20](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=680)).
- **Draw what serves the game.** Tile artists must draw what serves the player and the game, not what they feel like drawing. Ryan redrew Sil's werewolves as giant wolves possessed by spirits, per Tolkien, after first drawing humanoids, and gave cat assassins bows after noticing in play that they do not use daggers. Most of the demon-type uniques are fire-branded, so although Ryan wanted varied flavours for them, they were drawn to match ([Joel Ryan 2022, 18:15](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1095); [Joel Ryan 2022, 19:01](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1141)).

The same reasoning applies at other scales. Sea Of Rifts, seen mostly from a distant camera, exaggerates the proportions of features that matter for gameplay, such as an oversized weapon boom, accepting unrealistic shapes so players can always tell what is going on ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 12:21](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=741)).

### Scope cautions

Retrofitting tiles onto an existing game can be larger than it looks. Sil inherited broken tile code from NPP Angband: turning graphics on appeared to work, but tanglethorns showed as humans and an orc as a bag, and many monsters had no tile at all, which is how Ryan came to draw their own ([Joel Ryan 2022, 4:06](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=246)). Showing the wielded weapon on the player turned up 89 weapon combinations to fit into only 16 character tile slots per race, far more than expected, so Ryan drew 16 deliberately ambiguous tiles ([Joel Ryan 2022, 10:52](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=652)).

**A readability checklist for tile artists:**

- Can an experienced player read each tile by its two or three major forms? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442))
- Does the silhouette alone say what kind of threat this is? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 15:08](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=908))
- Have you kept size in reserve for the monsters that should feel dangerous? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 15:58](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=958))
- Do tiles and backgrounds differ in detail frequency, and does every tile carry the agreed outline? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 22:52](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1372); [Joel Ryan 2022, 21:33](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1293))
- Does colour carry consistent mechanical meaning, from one shared palette? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 19:01](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1141); [Joel Ryan 2022, 11:20](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=680))
- Does each tile match what the monster actually does in play? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 18:15](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1095))

## Creatures whose look says what they do

Roguelikes need many monsters, and each one has to teach the player something on sight.

### Design backwards from the mechanic

Justin Ma and Matthew Davis of Subset Games describe designing races and creatures backwards from their mechanics, picking obvious visuals that telegraph function: the high-health race is made of rock, the stabbing enemy is a praying mantis. They treat this as UX. Players do not have to memorise strange alien names or lore, or tell grey aliens from pink ones. Lapses happen: a "mosquito" enemy became a squid when the art changed and the name did not, which is a warning against placeholder names you do not expect to ship ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1576)). Marlowe Dobbe works the same way from the artist's side. Often a team knows how an enemy behaves before it has a look, and the look can be derived from that. Dobbe's example spec was a weak enemy doing small, multi-hit poisonous attacks with a defensive state when not attacking; they drew a sad-eyed, unintimidating creature with tentacles for the four quick hits, poison goo spilling from an upside-down cauldron, and the cauldron itself as the shell it retreats into ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 7:34](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=454)).

Dobbe also argues for quantity. Because roguelikes are replayed so often, players should not keep seeing the same three enemies; a large cast of visually distinct monsters, like the ones they drew for Dicey Dungeons and Floppy Knights, keeps repeated runs from feeling stale ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 2:08](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=128)).

### Showing state, not just identity

The same principle extends to simulation games, where art shows a creature's state as well as its kind. Liza Knipscher says the purpose of Bioloom's art direction is to give players the clearest possible picture of the underlying simulation data: whether a creature is young, old, sick, starving or dead, along with wet or snowy ground, atmospheric gases and fire. Its second goal is a cohesive stylised look that hides the seams where simulation objects are assembled ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=306)). Bioloom shows age by scaling each body part independently over a creature's life: heads and eyes start large and shrink, while horns, shells and branches start small and grow, so babies look like babies. It shows death by shrinking the skin away to reveal prefab bones of the same shape ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 11:57](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=717)).

Visual state can also change what an action means. Tabea Iseli's non-violent Grimoire Groves gives each plant creature several growth stages and detailed animations so players understand that their spells make plants grow and bloom, not hurt them; fully grown plants happily jump into the ground and spawn fruit. Iseli contrasts this with the usual flash-white-then-despawn hit feedback, which is enough only when players know they are killing things ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 19:36](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1176)).

### Producing many concepts

Dobbe's talk is a toolkit for generating enough monster ideas:

- **The list of 10.** Write the first ten ideas that come to mind without filtering, then combine a few inspiring words. Quality does not matter; a handful will be useful. From weeds, clouds and galactic Dobbe drew a floating, dandelion-like godlike being with cloud collars and star-shaped eyes in about 20 minutes ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 4:11](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=251)).
- **Reference is not cheating.** The line between inspiration and plagiarism is taking selected elements from many sources rather than copying one piece. Use several references at once (often 3 to 15 per enemy), favour styles different from your own, and never trace ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 11:12](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=672)).
- **Know what to extract.** Look for clothing and accessories, shapes and silhouettes, colour palettes, body types, rendering style and poses. A reference in a style far from your own is most useful because it removes the urge to copy one-for-one; you might take only its off-white palette or its fisheye angle ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 14:03](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=843)).
- **Keep a library.** Collect images, art books and photos (libraries and archive.org help when books are expensive), and keep local copies because nothing online is permanent ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 9:34](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=574)).

In a live demonstration Dobbe combined a castle tower, a big-headed character silhouette and a separate image's colour palette into a brick "castle bruiser" with a door-like tummy drawer and crenellated shoulders, unlike any of its three references. Without the palette reference they would have made a castle grey or brown, and the result already suggested mechanics, a heavy bruiser or giant ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 20:45](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=1245)). For a whole game's art direction Dobbe builds large mood boards of painters' styles and palettes, asks the team whether that is the vibe, and iterates from there ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 27:21](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=1641)).

Photography is another route to many expressive variants. Paris Buttfield-Addison describes how Hintline 93, after ruling out illustration as too costly, 3D as wrong for the period and full-motion video as too ambitious, photographed actors on green screen in many poses for each of about 23 emotions; each written line is tagged with a mood, and the game swaps photos as the caller talks ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:26:57](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23217)).

**In practice:** spec the mechanics first, then choose the visuals that teach them ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1576); [Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 7:34](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=454)); let state show on the body where your systems track it ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=306)); and generate concepts by combining parts of many references rather than waiting for one idea ([Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 11:12](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=672); [Marlowe Dobbe 2024, 20:45](https://youtu.be/Wi-OHFmW4Ew?t=1245)).

## Art on a budget: borrow, kitbash, keep it coherent

Small teams rarely have the art budget their content needs. The talks converge on one method, kitbashing, and one danger, incoherence.

### Kitbash from a small set of parts

Kitbashing, a term Phillip Daigle traces to sci-fi TV model makers combining parts from different model kits, means assembling new assets from pieces of existing ones ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 15:20](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=920)). Three speakers working on very different games arrive at it. Sergio Garces argues that a solo developer on a budget should build procedural 3D environments from pre-made pieces like LEGO rather than grow geometry from triangle maths, noise and fractals, which would take years; Garces notes that 3D artists kitbash even when nothing is procedural ([Sergio Garces 2022, 2:04](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=124)). Max Bottega's team gives each biome three or four small asset sets and smashes their pieces together into all of that biome's props, mostly keeping sets within their biome to preserve its identity; building the library is slow at first, then speeds work up dramatically ([Max Bottega 2024, 5:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=308)). Daigle, who cannot draw, kit-bashes open-licensed art that is almost right into assets that look bespoke, drawing on OpenGameArt.org (including the Stone Soup tileset and the cross-compatible Liberated Pixel Cup archive), Kenney's free assets and cheap paid tilesets ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 15:20](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=920)). For Rogue's Gate Daigle adopted the openly licensed art of Wyrmsun, an RTS on the Stratagus engine, because its sprites were split into layers that could be stacked into new sprites ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 19:08](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1148)).

Sofie Kjær Schmidt states the goal behind all of this for Sea Of Rifts: get the most visual variation from the fewest assets. That goal chose the game's top-down, low-poly style, which is quick to produce and allows variation, and led the team to look for corners to cut invisibly, such as texture swaps and colour variation ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 3:06](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=186)).

For a non-artist working in 2D there is another route. Evan Ovadia traces symbols and icons with the pen tool in a font editor (BirdFont, in their case) and renders them as outlined 3D meshes on tiles. During the 7DRL (a seven-day roguelike game jam) for Incendian Falls Ovadia traced a licensed icon set into the game in under 30 minutes, turning the most frustrating task into half an hour of tracing ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 2:16](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=136)).

### Coherence is the real constraint

The warning that accompanies every borrowing strategy is coherence. Garces calls it critical: asset flips fail because they slap together whatever is available, so match colour, polygon density and style, for example by buying from one vendor's consistent series or, as Garces did for Mekanical Armada, committing to realism so photogrammetry assets agree; watch for variance in quality too ([Sergio Garces 2022, 6:30](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=390)). Expect to replace the materials on purchased 3D assets with your own, both for a cohesive look and for technical reasons, since materials control colour, response to light and even vertex positions ([Sergio Garces 2022, 8:42](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=522)). Ovadia makes the 2D version of the point: without an artist you eventually need something your sprite sheet lacks, and reaching for other sheets is dangerous because their styles clash ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 5:16](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=316)). Sofie Kjær Schmidt adds the risks that are specific to bought assets: there are no source files to go back to, and the game can lose character and end up looking like a series of stock photos. Post-processing such as vignette and lighting helps bought and self-made assets sit together ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048)).

The two 3D speakers differ in emphasis about store assets. Garces argues they are a legitimate starting point, much as using a third-party engine once carried a stigma and no longer does; choosing an existing asset is like casting an actor rather than inventing one. Garces spent just over $2,000 on assets for Mekanical Armada and finds environments in particular quite doable this way ([Sergio Garces 2022, 4:02](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=242)). Kjær Schmidt finds bought assets useful for testing and speed but says to use them warily ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048)). The difference seems to depend on how far you will go to unify them: Garces plans to replace materials and keep to one style, Kjær Schmidt relies on post-processing to pull them together.

### Generating the presentation itself

Procedural generation can produce presentation as well as content. Thomas Robertson points out that games like Final Fantasy 7, with its limit breaks, and Pokémon, with 826 moves, could hire many artists to give every move its own presentation; roguelike developers cannot, but they can use procgen to generate many unique super-attack presentations, which Robertson presents as a work in progress ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 1:35](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=95)). Generation also creates new presentation problems. Courtney Liessen notes that ability upgrades are usually quantised, say +20% radius, with custom effects for each upgraded version, and players assume art comes in a few fixed tiers. A 2x radius multiplier that stacks with other multipliers breaks that assumption, raising the question of whether an ability could cover the whole screen; Hades and Vampire Survivors have effects that scale heavily in this way ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 7:00](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=420)).

**In practice:** pick one style and one main source, kitbash within it from small reusable sets ([Sergio Garces 2022, 6:30](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=390); [Max Bottega 2024, 5:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=308)), take ownership of materials and post-processing so the pieces agree ([Sergio Garces 2022, 8:42](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=522); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048)), and if your numbers can grow without bound, plan effects that scale with them ([Courtney Liessen 2024, 7:00](https://youtu.be/BRJEK20iM7o?t=420)).

## Making generated spaces look art-directed

Max Bottega names the problem plainly: procedurally generated environments often look completely random and not good, because it is hard to encode visual logic into how a generator places things. Bottega's answer, on a small budget, was not a smarter generator but hand-dressed tiles and art-side rules ([Max Bottega 2024, 1:02](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=62)). The fixes collected here follow that approach: let the generator place, and let art rules compose.

### Direct the eye

A library in which every prop is unique and eye-catching distracts the player. Bottega's team practises what the talk calls "uniform variation": small and medium generic props plus three or four hero pieces per set, with each tile dressed with one or two hero props surrounded by generic props of the same volume, then grass or bushes to blend them in ([Max Bottega 2024, 9:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=548)). Loren Schmidt arrives at a related principle from terrain generation: vary spatial frequency, mixing large gestural forms with finely detailed areas, because an image with the same frequency everywhere is jarring and gives the eye nowhere to rest ([Loren Schmidt 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1858)). Both are saying that attention needs contrast: a few focal points among quieter material.

### Ground the props

Props dropped onto a flat plane look like wargame models. Bottega's props stand "on their own feet": each has three layers, the core asset, a base piece of ground matched to the environment, and pebbles, grass and small bushes that diminish in size and number outward. Cluster that debris, since nature does not distribute objects uniformly ([Max Bottega 2024, 7:18](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=438)). Walls are the exception to the hero-and-generic rule: each is a single self-contained low-poly mesh that already includes its ground-blending debris, such as pebbles or bones, so it can be slammed onto any tile and work without adjustment, which matters because so many must be placed ([Max Bottega 2024, 10:00](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=600)). To keep biomes from looking like different games, Bottega set up a single camera that collected five proportional slices from cameras looking at different biomes, and tuned materials while looking through it so colours and gradients stayed compatible ([Max Bottega 2024, 10:33](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=633)).

### Procedural dressing over hand-made structure

Sébastien "deepnight" Benard splits the work the other way round in Dead Cells: rooms are hand-made, but decoration is fully procedural, painted on by a "decorator" algorithm that follows biome rules. Because the game is about combat, not examining backgrounds, a decent procedural background was good enough, and it freed time for other work ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1048)). Benard's level editor LDtk applies the same idea to tiling: the designer marks only semantics such as collision or water, and rules paint grass, corners and the rest automatically ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 8:56](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=536)).

### Shader-driven variety

Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt describe several shader techniques from Sea Of Rifts that multiply a few assets into many:

- **HSV colour swaps.** An HSV-offset shader with a database of colour swaps recolours ships from only three texture atlases, producing many variants that also tell players which faction a ship belongs to ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 16:27](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=987)). Human-made objects, including asset-store models, use a texture mask that applies HSV offsets per region ([Alexander Birke 2024, 7:50](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=470)).
- **A per-object hash.** Because the world streams and x/z coordinates shift, the only constant per-object data is height and rotation. A dot product plus `fmod` over the world matrix turns these into a deterministic random value that offsets colour and window lighting, so houses get slightly different tints. Up close this would be unrealistic; on a small screen it reads as natural variation instead of flat dullness ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 19:02](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1142); [Alexander Birke 2024, 7:50](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=470)).
- **Sub-tiling trim sheets.** A shader combines trim sheets with nine-slicing by storing a tile offset and tile dimensions in vertex data, then offsetting the UV and repeating it at the tile frequency, so one tile set shows many textures without stretching to the edge. Tiles bleed at lower mip levels; pad each tile with itself, which a custom texture importer can automate ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 24:38](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1478)).

Their conclusion is that shaders can add a lot of variety to a small selection of props and are an area with much room for exploration in procedural games, alongside finding where your camera lets you cut corners invisibly ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 32:15](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1935)).

### Plan the lighting

Generated 3D layouts rule out one standard tool. Sergio Garces warns that pre-baked light maps cannot be computed for layouts that do not exist until runtime, so procedural 3D needs dynamic lighting, and each dynamic light adds per-pixel cost. A single directional sun light with partly dynamic shadows performed well for Mekanical Armada in Unreal Engine 4, and Unreal Engine 5's Lumen offers real-time global illumination; but a game full of static lights, such as a torch-lit dungeon, should plan its lighting early ([Sergio Garces 2022, 22:03](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1323)).

**In practice:**

- Dress each generated chunk with one or two focal props among generic ones, and vary detail density across the map ([Max Bottega 2024, 9:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=548); [Loren Schmidt 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1858)).
- Give every prop and wall its own ground and clustered debris so it blends wherever it lands ([Max Bottega 2024, 7:18](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=438); [Max Bottega 2024, 10:00](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=600)).
- Compare biomes side by side while tuning colour ([Max Bottega 2024, 10:33](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=633)).
- Use rules or a decorator to dress hand-made structure ([Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=1048); [Sébastien "deepnight" Benard 2025, 8:56](https://youtu.be/QbTnKvRrNYY?t=536)).
- Get variation from shaders keyed to stable per-object data ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 19:02](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1142); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 32:15](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1935)).
- Decide your lighting model before you fill dungeons with torches ([Sergio Garces 2022, 22:03](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=1323)).

## Juice: making turns feel alive

Everything so far has been about how the world looks when it stands still. The rest of the chapter is about what moves and what sounds, starting with the motion that follows each turn.

When a turn resolves, the state of a grid game jumps from one position to the next. The talks' answer to making that jump feel like something happened is *juice*, and Jeremiah Reid is clear that it is neither expensive nor reserved for action games ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 3:42](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=222)).

### What juice is

Chris McCormick equates juice with game feel: the combination of sound and animation that happens in response to input and makes a game feel alive, with screen shake as the textbook case ([Chris McCormick 2021, 3:56](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=236)). Jeremiah Reid's definition is close but wider. Reid quotes the formula "maximum output for minimum input" and pushes back on the idea that juice is mechanically superfluous: it is usually visual or auditory, but it does not have to be, and mechanics and text can be juicy too ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 2:01](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=121)).

Reid's most useful claim for a roguelike developer is about cost. Juice is "coded in, not drawn in": almost all of it is interpolating scale, position, rotation and colour towards a target, so a solo programmer with no art skills can do it. A generic tween that moves a property towards a target is about 30 lines in a dynamic language ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 9:22](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=562)). The advice comes from regret. Reid held off juicing Golden Krone Hotel in its first years because they did not know the techniques existed, assumed they were harder than they are, and thought juice belonged to action games rather than traditional roguelikes; all three assumptions were wrong, and they believe earlier juice would have drawn a bigger audience sooner ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 3:42](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=222)).

### The technique kit

Reid's talk is a step-by-step kit for a grid game. In the order you would build it:

- **Easing.** Linear and exponential easing cover most roguelike needs. To move a sprite from tile A to tile B, you shrink the remaining delta towards zero; linear easing does it at constant speed, exponential easing shaves a fixed percentage (say 10%) off the remaining delta every frame, so the sprite moves fast at first and settles gently on the target ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 10:56](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=656)).
- **Per-step move queues and a lagging camera.** If you animate all of a turn's movement in one go, a monster that turned a corner slides diagonally, so queue each tile-to-tile step separately. Tie the camera to the player's *animated* position rather than their logical one to remove jerkiness, and let it follow with a slight lag so it feels less stiff ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 14:31](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=871)).
- **Squash, stretch and hop.** Borrowing from the 7DRL game Acatha in Absurdia, Reid has the character crouch short and wide, then stretch tall and thin, looping even while idle, and moves it between tiles on a parabolic hop in z. A little bounce, they say, makes a turn-based game feel dramatically better ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 16:02](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=962)).
- **Anticipation.** A slight lean in the direction of travel and a short delay before leaving the tile, like the crouch before a jump, make movement feel poppy; tuning the delay changes how sticky or bouncy it feels ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 17:52](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1072)).
- **Directional screen shake.** Basic shake randomises the camera's x and y. Following Crypt of the NecroDancer, Reid nudges the camera towards the enemy when the player attacks, so it feels like leaning into the blow, and shakes the camera's rotation when the player is hit, as if slapped ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 20:12](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1212)).
- **Hit flashes and damage numbers.** A white flash on being hit, damage numbers in every game regardless of how much other juice it has, and crits drawn at double size ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 20:56](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1256)).
- **Leave traces.** Make the player's actions visibly change the world: Reid's demo leaves corpses, and later sends killed enemies flying through the air with rotation ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 21:29](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1289)).

> Every game regardless of what you're doing with juice, you need to have damage numbers. — [Jeremiah Reid 2021, 20:56](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1256)

### Layering, and mechanics that are juice

No single effect makes the difference; the stack does. McCormick counts seven effects visible at once in Oolong's Chicken Sword demo: a dust trail, moving grass, a lamp that swings when bumped, muzzle flash, recoil, a visible shot and smoke as the shot expires, and argues that the accumulation of small reactions is what creates the feeling ([Chris McCormick 2021, 4:36](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=276)). Reid calls a three-second clip of Fidel Dungeon Rescue's level-up a master class: the "level up" text alone has around ten things animating, and the moment also feels good mechanically because levelling refills health and adds a heart ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 6:21](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=381)). That second half is Reid's point about juicy mechanics. Their favourite is Jupiter Hell's shotgun and revolver reload, one shell at a time, which they copy into their demo along with cheap sound effects made from free sounds or a sound generator ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 22:54](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1374)).

### Juice in the browser

McCormick shows how to retrofit this onto a roguelike built with rot.js, the JavaScript roguelike library, which by default draws everything into one canvas that behaves like a single giant image. Position an HTML div over the canvas and update its position in the entity's draw function; the div then tracks the entity and can carry sparkles, dust or bounce, render the character itself so it moves independently of the grid, or receive click handlers ([Chris McCormick 2021, 20:26](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1226)). In Smallest Quest McCormick draws backgrounds with rot.js and renders characters and items as floating divs whose bobbing, jumping and sword-swipe overlays are short, declarative CSS animations added by class ([Chris McCormick 2021, 21:43](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1303)). McCormick's commercial game Asteroid is mechanically smaller and simpler than Rogue but graphically richer, with screen shake, monster ghosts, hit point indicators and items that pop off the top of the screen when collected ([Chris McCormick 2021, 5:20](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=320)).

### The limits: tone, violence and blocking

Juice has a tone, and it can be the wrong one. Reid notes their own game involves drinking blood off the floor, so silliness fits; a game like Infra Arcana might not want bouncy techniques at all. Asked about misuse, they name animations that block the player and notes that some players found Teleglitch too much ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:00](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1620)).

The standard canon also assumes violence. Tabea Iseli, whose plant growth stages appeared earlier in this chapter, marked up the Art of Screenshake techniques for Grimoire Groves, and found that almost half relate directly to weapons, explosions or impact. They are not useless (a plant can play a hit animation when it receives energy), but the team had to build the feel of growing and energising from scratch ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 10:34](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=634)). Their equivalent of adding bass to a gun was making energised plants laugh, chuckle and cheer: starting from a coin-pickup "bling" and cranking it up, they found that giving the plants' faces happy vocal reactions was a complete game changer ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 28:20](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=1700)).

Whether juice competes with depth is unresolved. McCormick keeps their own games minimal for lack of time, but would like to see a deep classic such as NetHack heavily juiced ([Chris McCormick 2021, 30:28](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1828)).

### An edge case: animation under rollback

Juice assumes the past is fixed. In a game with rollback netcode it is not. Adrian Zeyfang describes how Synchrony, Crypt of the NecroDancer's multiplayer, keeps movement smooth when turns are resimulated: idle animations are stateless, computed from local music time, while each move copies a global animation timer into a per-turn buffer and interpolates from it. Each animation gets a stable identity of entity, turn ID and animation name, so when a move is resimulated its existing start time is kept rather than restarted. A global move counter would not work as the ID, because rollback shifts it and scrambles the animations ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 17:50](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=1070)).

**In practice:** add juice early, not in year three; write one generic tween and build everything from it; animate per step and never block input on an animation; and pick effects that match the game's tone and what its verbs are actually about.

## Sound design for games that are mostly symbols

Juice is sound as well as motion, yet most roguelikes have little or none ([Josh Ge 2016, 17:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1034)), and the talks that address sound treat that as a missed opportunity rather than a neutral default.

### Why symbol-minded designers are suited to sound

Julian K. Jarboe opens bluntly: if you think sound, including its absence, is not an important or meaningful part of your game, you are mistaken. Their argument for why roguelike developers in particular should take it on is that they already have the key skill: they understand that simple, abstract symbols can convey an enormous amount, and they like to tinker. Talent, software and time help but are not required ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 1:12](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=72)). Josh Ge makes the complementary argument from Cogmind: sound effects support the player's imagination of an ASCII world without hijacking it the way detailed visuals do. Few roguelikes have audio; Cogmind has over 1,000 samples where most have about zero, and what Ge asks for is effects and atmosphere rather than music ([Josh Ge 2016, 17:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1034)). Cogmind's machines emit ambient sound by distance and direction, so you can hear things around a corner that you cannot yet see, which both builds atmosphere and carries information ([Josh Ge 2016, 19:49](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1189)).

Jarboe widens the frame further. Sound design is more than music and effects: atmospheric sound often fits neither category, can be simple and subtle, and a game need not include music or effects at all. The sounds of the player's own environment, including those they make, are part of their experience of your design too ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 4:37](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=277)). Players listen, or wear headphones, for many reasons, from blocking out the world to asserting personal space while listening to nothing. Understand those reasons, accept that some players will mute your game, and at least make something you would want to listen to yourself; your own sensory quirks are assets that form your style ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 3:15](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=195)).

### A process for finding the sound

Jarboe treats genre or mood as a promise to players and listeners. To find what that promise sounds like, they adapt a worksheet written for fiction podcast writers: list the sounds you associate with the setting, ask which music, machines, animals, weather and people are present or absent and why, consider what makes them feel like the genre, and imagine the real world tomorrow sounding like only those things ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 7:06](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=426)).

From there, Jarboe's process notes are practical:

- **Feel-accurate, not accurate.** A punch sells better as snapped celery than as a recording of a real boxing match ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 3:27](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=207)).
- **Everything counts as procedural, and nothing is cheating.** Procedural sound covers software that composes a sonata and a script that picks a random recorded burp from a folder. Collaging assets you have the rights to until they are your own, using free assets, and hiring collaborators are all legitimate ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 4:05](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=245)).
- **Audio sprites.** Just as with visual sprites, you can bundle a small library of sounds and reuse them with effects modified on the fly, which suits limited budgets ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 5:52](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=352)).
- **Mix carefully.** Use the best over-ear headphones you can rather than earbuds, learn basic frequency bands so you can fix muddy overlaps without cutting sounds, and prioritise consistent volume over consistent quality: you cannot always control quality, but you can control volume, and it matters more ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 6:48](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=408)).
- **Understand MIDI.** Lots of public-domain music exists as MIDI and is very easy to adapt ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 6:46](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=406)).

> It needs to feel accurate, not be accurate. If you want that punch to sound like a punch, you're better off snapping celery. — [Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 3:27](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=207)

### Feedback sounds say something

A feedback sound is a statement, not a neutral confirmation. Xalavier Nelson Jr. describes Space Warlord Organ Trading Simulator's three quest-completion sounds: positive, neutral and negative. The neutral one sounds like an error, so most quests default to positive. But the player is a cutthroat participant in an exploitative organ market, so when a quest for a philanthropic hospital administrator is fulfilled, a positive sound endorses a view, and a negative one says something about the character and about a world hostile to helping anyone but misanthropes ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 17:00](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1020)). Choose each feedback sound for what it tells the player about the act, not only that the act succeeded.

### Voice: generate it, don't splice it

Two independent talks converge on the same warning about voice. Paul Dean, asked what does not work non-linearly, named voice audio first: recorded performance does not survive being chopped up and rearranged, because inflection is too organic to slice, and even a chopped robot voice would not work well ([Paul Dean 2025, 26:19](https://youtu.be/nLqLOzrjkYU?t=1579)). Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick learned the same thing on Neutrinowatch, a podcast that generates itself: splicing recorded performances became too complex with a big branching script and sounded off, so they moved to text-to-speech, using standard Apple voices for robot characters and voice models of the hosts for the human ones ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 12:51](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=771)). Generating audio in code also means rebuilding the DAW (digital audio workstation): Austwick describes translating cutting, layering, fades, echo, filters, pitch shift and shared reverb into Python, and notes that putting the same reverb on many clips makes them sound like they happened in one space, which is how scenes are built ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 11:23](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=683)).

### Sound under rollback

Like animation, sound breaks when the past can be rewritten. Zeyfang explains that Synchrony tracks sound effects per turn. On rollback, each sound in the turn's list is marked "for stop or awaiting recurrence"; sounds that recur in the resimulation keep playing without being retriggered, new ones play, and anything still marked at the end of the turn is cut. In Zeyfang's example a player's hurt sound is cut because, after rollback, their earlier attack killed the skeleton first. This matters most for long sounds such as player deaths and boss phase transitions, because the goal is that rollback never gives misleading audio feedback about a significant event ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 20:43](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=1243)).

**In practice:** design the soundscape deliberately, including its silences; start with a small reusable library of feel-accurate sounds; keep volume consistent; make every feedback sound say what you mean; and do not plan on splicing recorded voice.

## Music that survives a thousand runs

A roguelike's music is heard far more often than most games', and the same loop on run two hundred is a different experience from run one.

### The problem: ear fatigue

Crashtroid, a composer, names the problem *ear fatigue*: hearing something so often or so loud that its frequencies blur together and become hard to distinguish, the way a composer's ears go when looping a section while mixing. Because roguelikes are played over and over, their music is especially prone to it, and Crashtroid wants players to stay engaged with the score across runs rather than be worn out by a shop theme heard a million times ([Crashtroid 2023, 2:56](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=176)). The talk offers three remedies.

### Segment the loop

First, write loops with distinctly segmented sections, so the player feels progress through the loop instead of letting it melt into the background ([Crashtroid 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=226)). Sections can be classic intro and chorus structure, or even a radio system that swaps songs midway. In The Binding of Isaac's "Repentant", four sections add chords, then vocals, then a piano ending that lifts to a major chord suggesting a chance to survive ([Crashtroid 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=226)). Segmentation can be subtler: Crashtroid's own final-stage theme for Peglin changes the solo instrument and the drum line between sections, and key changes work too ([Crashtroid 2023, 6:37](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=397)).

### Pace the music to play, not just to the look

Second, pace music to the moment-to-moment gameplay, not only to the game's aesthetic, and ideally let the composer play a prototype. The main thing players do is play, and their actions shape how they hear the audio ([Crashtroid 2023, 8:19](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=499)). Crashtroid's comparison is two combat shooter roguelikes with very different scores: in Roboquest's fast arena-shooter music they noticed the beats per minute lining up with bunny hopping and gun fire rates (they do not know whether by design), while Risk of Rain 2's music emphasises exploration and discovery on a sprawling planet, because that is what its players spend their time doing ([Crashtroid 2023, 10:48](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=648)).

### Avoid jarring cuts, and use transitions as signposts

Third, avoid jarring cuts, which matter more in long or repeated runs (citing speedrunners and three-hour runs). Use alternate versions of a track that fade into each other, such as Borderlands' ambient and combat variants, and let the areas of a map share a melody in cut-down passive versions for cohesion ([Crashtroid 2023, 12:00](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=720)). Crashtroid's reading of Hades shows how transitions can carry information: stage music fades between ambient and combat versions, a stinger concludes a song, silence follows until the next room, where a new song marks roughly the one-third point; the pattern repeats after the miniboss and the boss. It is a quiet way of telling the player they are making progress, and the talk recommends flowcharting your own music like this to find gaps that break immersion ([Crashtroid 2023, 13:43](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=823)).

Jon Perry gives a convergent example from UFO 50's Mini and Max, where distinct music plays when the player enters a handcrafted area. Perry considers this key signposting, because otherwise a player might enter from one side, not realise the spot matters, and leave before reaching its key part ([Jon Perry 2025, 12:19](https://youtu.be/NlxGPKV0PrY?t=739)). Martin Pichlmair's analysis of The Legend of Zelda explains why sequenced rather than prerecorded audio makes this kind of responsiveness easy: rule-based melody transitions, timing to events, and raising intensity by adding structure or instruments, at the cost of never sounding as full as an orchestra ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 22:32](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1352)).

### Test it and time it

Crashtroid's closing test is simple:

> If you can't listen to the song more than 15 minutes at a time outside the game, it probably won't work inside the game. — [Crashtroid 2023, 15:01](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=901)

Two smaller points concern resourcing. Santiago Zapata found background music a large help for mood and credits DoomRL with pioneering the practice; building on existing universes (Castlevania, Metroid) made it possible to use music found online without an artist ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 7:44](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=464)). Phillip Daigle says audio is a good place to bring in a collaborator, but not too early: scoring Rogue's Gate while its direction swung from sci-fi ship shooter to Baldur's Gate clone in a week frustrated Daigle's musician friend, and open-source audio covered most needs until then ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 20:13](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=1213)).

**In practice:**

- Give every loop audible sections so a listener can tell where in it they are.
- Write to the rhythm of play (fire rates, exploration pace), which means playing the game first.
- Provide ambient and combat variants that crossfade, and share motifs across an area.
- Use stingers, silence and new themes as progress markers; flowchart them.
- Apply the 15-minute listening test.
- Bring a composer in once the game's direction has settled.

## Generative music: motifs, rhythms and the composer's hand

Looping fixed tracks is one answer to repetition; generating the music is another. The talks that try it each build a small representation suited to one game, and differ mainly on how much the human should curate what it produces.

### The composer is still needed

Paul Hembree's central claim is that a single generative rule is never enough. One Euclidean rhythm alone does not make interesting music; the solution, they say, is to be a composer: curate a stylistic subset of the parameter space (powers of two or multiples of three for common time, primes for asymmetrical meters) and layer and segment the results with other rhythms, using some as accent patterns ([Paul Hembree 2026, 19:46](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1186)).

The history is old. Pichlmair describes the musical dice games attributed to Mozart (who had no hand in them; the name was branding): roll two dice, look up a number in a table, and it points to a pre-written fragment; assemble the fragments and play them live. It is controlled random composition, and Pichlmair notes that a grammar tool like Tracery could assemble music the same way ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 20:41](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1241)).

### Euclidean rhythms, implemented simply

A *Euclidean rhythm* spreads k onsets as evenly as possible over n time slots (for example, 3 hits in 8). Hembree's one takeaway is that they are an efficient way to represent a very large set of syncopated rhythms without machine learning ([Paul Hembree 2026, 4:17](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=257)). You do not need Bjorklund's algorithm to make them: they are equivalent to an evenly spaced tuplet quantised to a grid, which producers do every day. For each note index, multiply by the numerator, divide by the denominator, and round with a floor function plus a rounding point. Played unquantised, a 5-in-12 tuplet sounds like an unrelated rhythmic layer; quantised with a rounding point of 0.2, one note snaps forward and it suddenly grooves ([Paul Hembree 2026, 10:12](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=612)).

The rounding point is also a control. Where Toussaint rotated Euclidean rhythms like necklaces on a clock face, Hembree raises the rounding point from 0 upwards (even past 1, to start on rests), which moves one note at a time, giving a perceptually smooth walk through a family of related rotations; Hembree demonstrates stepping through the rotations of the son clave ([Paul Hembree 2026, 15:21](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=921)). There is a ceiling: the charm of these rhythms comes from failing to be perfectly even, so as the grid gets finer the difference from the pure tuplet shrinks and the syncopation vanishes. In a listening test from 5:8 to 5:32 they hear a categorical shift, and suggests about 24 slots as an upper limit at medium and fast tempos ([Paul Hembree 2026, 17:44](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1064)).

To enrich the patterns Hembree applies substitution systems that work like musical ornaments: *allative* ones prepend short notes leading into a long one, *ablative* ones replace a long note with trailing short ones. Applying allative ornaments to one pattern produced the Afro-Caribbean bembe, which is also a 7-in-12 Euclidean rhythm; they admit choosing that example for this reason, but say that if you apply ornaments algorithmically you will find such rhythms all over the place ([Paul Hembree 2026, 20:51](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1251)).

Finally, Hembree separates generation from selection. Because these rhythms are just quantisation they are extremely cheap, so the beat generator renders thousands of candidates per second and matches them against perception-based controls: density, durational variance, syncopation (measured as offbeatness, the simplest of about 15 competing definitions) and irregularity. Keeping controls apart from the generator makes it possible to improve either side independently ([Paul Hembree 2026, 24:27](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1467)).

### Motifs as recipes: Tea Garden

Sonat Uzun's Tea Garden takes a different representation. In a game about decorating a garden with generated flowers and visiting generated dream worlds, procedural music fits because players can discover music they like the way they discover flowers ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 3:22](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=202)). Uzun's motif-based generation identifies the important aspects of the music, defines a pool of possible motifs for each, and picks randomly. A motif is a looping string of numbers and symbols written note by note into PICO-8's music memory; there are motif pools not only for melody, arpeggio, bass, kick and snare but for effects, instruments and volume, and combining one from each yields a part ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 13:32](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=812)).

> Motifs are just recipes and in order to cook we should add context. — [Sonat Uzun 2022, 16:58](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1018)

The context is harmonic: a scale, chords that are subsets of it, and a randomly chosen chord progression. Melodies use only scale notes, arpeggios only chord tones, and switching major to minor changes the vibe a great deal ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 16:58](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1018)). Variation comes from shift motifs that transpose a whole motif and from special symbols: X for silence, B to begin the loop, J to jump to a random position, S to change speed, D to target a chord tone below, O for an octave up, and any further behaviour you need can get its own symbol ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 19:54](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1194)). One source of variety was an accident: cramming up to six parts into PICO-8's three channels makes voices block each other, so a snare can swallow a melody note, and an arpeggio combined with a kick yields a pattern unlike the arpeggio alone. Uzun found these collisions often sound intentional and kept them ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 21:35](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1295)).

### How much to trust randomness

Here the two composers differ.
