Uzun steers mood with a light hand, picking distinctive scales (spooky ones, say) and motifs with more silences, and otherwise trusts randomness to produce something good; the songs showcased in the talk came from barely curated random motifs ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 28:45](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1725)). Hembree insists on curation as the composer's job ([Paul Hembree 2026, 19:46](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1186)). What they share matters as much: Uzun built the generator for Tea Garden specifically, not as an all-genres tool, though they think its methods transfer ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 6:07](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=367)), and Hembree's curation is likewise a choice of one style. The amount of curation you need probably depends on how narrow your representation already is: Uzun's scales and chord tones constrain the output before randomness touches it.

### Devices and toys: Rhythm Doggo

Nifflas builds music software for Rhythm Doggo out of playful devices rather than a grammar. A "rainbow" arpeggiator performs a real-time sort on its note array one step at a time, then reverse-sorts it, so a repeated melody slowly mutates and the player hears a slightly changed variation each time they walk through a door ([Nifflas 2025, 5:20](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=320)). Nifflas turns everyday situations into algorithms: a railway device switches tracks with some chance per note, and a train-stop device, inspired by three hours stuck in train traffic, queues notes like stalled trains that then rush through to catch up, giving odd rhythmic feels ([Nifflas 2025, 12:48](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=768)). A reflector device spawns cursors that bounce around a grid of squares, always reflecting off white squares and only probabilistically off intermediate ones, producing semi-predictable percussion ([Nifflas 2025, 7:25](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=445)). They have even composed melodies by simulating repeated Monty Hall problems under configurable host assumptions (is the host evil, do they know where the car is, are they in a hurry); in the game's own Monty Hall encounter, the randomised car position is the algorithm playing the music ([Nifflas 2025, 19:35](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=1175)).

### Keep humans in the loop

Hembree's last point concerns tools. The generator exports MP3 and MIDI so you can take the material into a DAW with your own sounds; a small tool that outputs editable material is meant as a provocation to build on, not as something "so large that it replaces your entire workflow". Hembree contrasts that deliberately limited scope with Suno, which they say scraped the internet, their own work included ([Paul Hembree 2026, 29:34](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1774)).

**In practice:** choose one compact representation (Euclidean rhythms, motif strings, devices); constrain it with your style (scales, ratios, slot limits) ([Paul Hembree 2026, 17:44](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1064); [Sonat Uzun 2022, 16:58](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1018)); layer several outputs rather than trusting one rule ([Paul Hembree 2026, 19:46](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1186)); generate many candidates and filter by perceptual measures if you can ([Paul Hembree 2026, 24:27](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1467)); and export editable material so a person can finish it ([Paul Hembree 2026, 29:34](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1774)).

## Music bound to the world and the game state

Generated levels raise a problem that linear games do not have. Paul Hembree states it directly: in a generated dungeon with branches and loops, players move in and out of psychological states through monsters, treasure and visual change in an order nobody knows in advance, so you cannot compose a linear piece guaranteed to underscore that succession. Horizontal resequencing and vertical remixing exist, but Hembree proposes tying music to the world's coordinate system instead ([Paul Hembree 2023, 3:55](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=235)). Big events such as a character's death still deserve big musical arrivals, but exploration is itself a traversal of psychological states, and composers can underscore it by subtly changing the scales, harmony or melodic material as the player moves ([Paul Hembree 2023, 1:48](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=108)).

### Discovery built into tonality

Hembree's analytical example is Kenji Yamamoto's Norfair music in Super Metroid. It alternates Phrygian chords a semitone apart and transposes up three semitones each section. Each such modulation keeps four pitches and adds three, so it reaches all twelve pitches in four modulations instead of twelve steps round the circle of fifths. The modulations underscore movement and ratchet tension with each ascent ([Paul Hembree 2023, 10:37](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=637)).

> The aesthetic of surprise and discovery is thus embedded in the tonal framework of the music. — [Paul Hembree 2023, 10:37](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=637)

### Pitch lattices as maps

The tool for binding harmony to space is a *pitch lattice*, a spatial model that places related pitches near each other. Hembree surveys Shepard's double helix and the Euler/Riemann lattice tiled by intervals of seven and four semitones; in such spaces, short-range relations act like harmonies and medium-range ones like scales. Square or cubic lattices are the most useful for game designers because they line up with standard 2D and 3D coordinates. "Related" usually means consonant, but could deliberately mean dissonant, for survival horror say ([Paul Hembree 2023, 7:31](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=451)).

### Rite of Tephra, step by step

Hembree's Rite of Tephra is a worked implementation:

1. **Lattice.** A cubic lattice of pitch nodes is overlaid on the level, 36 metres apart, a distance calibrated to walking pace so harmony shifts neither too fast nor too slow. Pitch C sits at the origin; each axis transposes by a chosen interval, summed and wrapped modulo 12. The nodes nearest the player set the music's scale and also the colour of light-emitting objects, with pitch classes mapped onto the RGB colour wheel along the circle of fifths ([Paul Hembree 2023, 16:12](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=972)).
2. **Hearing radius.** Pitch classes fade in and out within a 52-metre sphere around the player, reaching full volume at 24 metres on a half-cosine curve. The radius is chosen so seven to eight nodes are audible at once, the size of a typical scale; a bigger sphere would hear eleven, a smaller one only one. Hembree stresses this is not realistic attenuation but a musically pleasing control of abstract qualities ([Paul Hembree 2023, 17:11](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=1031)).
3. **Tiling per level.** Hembree hand-selected a subset of lattice tilings that sound appealing and picks one at random for each level, so each cave explores a different pitch space. A tiling's character can be summarised by a centred scale (player on a node, hearing its six neighbours) and an equidistant scale (player at a cube's centre, hearing eight corners); other positions blend the two ([Paul Hembree 2023, 18:15](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=1095)).
4. **Stems, not notes.** Rather than composing just in time, the game live-remixes pre-composed orchestral stems, one per pitch class, fading in those matching nearby nodes. This allowed high-quality orchestral samples, with in-game reverb smoothing transitions. The costs are real: rhythms are baked into each stem, every combination has to work texturally, and stepwise melodies became extremely hard to rely on ([Paul Hembree 2023, 18:38](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=1118)).
5. **Phasing loops.** Each stem runs the same ordered chain of events (drones, morse-like signals, outbursts, octave leaps, separated by empty space) at different speeds and offsets, so the loops phase against each other and chords and melodies emerge from their interaction. Hembree likens it to moiré patterns, or to a mobile activated by the player's movement ([Paul Hembree 2023, 19:42](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=1182)).

### Other bindings: levels, code hooks and data

You do not need a lattice to tie music to state. Nifflas's Rhythm Doggo exposes controls to game code: a step sequencer's cursor jumps randomly by an amount set by a "chaos" node (0 plays normally, 1 jumps wildly), and naming a group of nodes (the example given is "fish") lets the game reference and drive them directly ([Nifflas 2025, 3:14](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=194)). Asked about director systems for tension, Nifflas says long-term intensity lives in the level, not the music software: they place many songs throughout the level in their editor so any progress enters a new musical stage, with local tweaks such as raising intensity on a particular platform ([Nifflas 2025, 27:47](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=1667)). That is the same answer as Crashtroid's and Perry's signposting in the previous section, reached from the generative side.

Tyler Coleman notes that FFT (fast Fourier transform) analysis, overall energy plus frequency bands for kick, hat and snare, can turn audio into almost any game parameter, and points to the reverse, sonifying game state, as the approach of Mini Metro's music, which grows as the player's map grows ([Tyler Coleman 2026, 5:28:46](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=19726)). Isaac Io Schankler's Orb Pondering Simulator binds sound to a single variable for a non-game purpose: a sound gets louder as an orb grows and quieter as it shrinks, pacing box breathing (in as it grows, hold, out as it shrinks); the ERROR entities breathe at a different rate, so following them could make you hyperventilate ([Isaac Io Schankler 2024, 1:35](https://youtu.be/M6t5W5PPVW0?t=95)).

**In practice:** pick the game variable the music should follow (position, progress, map size, danger); make the mapping musical rather than physically realistic; calibrate its rate to how fast players actually move; and let level design carry long-term intensity where the music system cannot.

## Pushing the medium

The sections so far describe practice. This one collects provocations and experiments: directions the talks point to, not established techniques.

### The typewriter challenge

Nick Montfort's 2016 talk sets the challenge. Concrete poetry arranges letters so the layout carries the meaning; a poem that repeats "silence" around a gap is inverted if you read it aloud, and groups like Noigandres used the regularity and shape of the typed page to engage with language visually ([Nick Montfort 2016, 13:45](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=825)). Steve McCaffery's Carnival, made on a typewriter around 1970, pushes further with "dirty concrete": McCaffery rotated the page on the platen, masked letters to type only part of them, and overtyped in red and black, producing architectural, undulating spaces that look like a dungeon map while staying legible text ([Nick Montfort 2016, 14:53](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=893)). Before McCaffery, Dom Sylvester Houédard used fine horizontal microspacing to make three-dimensional-looking forms from perhaps two characters, which Montfort calls more Fez-like than roguelike ([Nick Montfort 2016, 17:39](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=1059)).

One distinction in the talk sharpens the earlier argument about what abstraction does for the player. Montfort distinguishes ASCII art, which uses characters to depict a picture, from concrete poetry and roguelikes, which engage with space and give letters new meanings, though roguelikes do it on a more rectilinear grid than the typewriter poets ([Nick Montfort 2016, 18:55](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=1135)). The challenge is to do with the computer display what McCaffery did with the typewriter and make a roguelike as stunning for the computer as Carnival is for the typewriter; asked whether any roguelike already pushes ASCII that way, Montfort could not name one ([Nick Montfort 2016, 16:37](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=997)).

### Re-rendering the same world

Several projects treat the renderer as a material rather than a window. Todd Furmanski's Forska post-processes its real-time render so one procedural world can look like a Roman mosaic, an oil painting or ASCII art, to escape the sameness of plain polygon rendering; in Unity they layer a mosaic effect, depth separation of foreground and background, and blended overlays, and notes the approach can hit the limits of legibility ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 10:31](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=631)). Chelsea Thompto renders Three.js 3D spaces live as ASCII characters for the opposite reason to most graphics work: to make the digital materiality of the space obvious and undercut realistic immersion in favour of immersion in an idea ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 8:19](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=499)).

Constraint can be pushed too. Greg L shows a screen-space bloom on PICO-8 in about 3 ms per frame, roughly a fifth of a frame. PICO-8's 16 on-screen colours can be remapped from 32, which allows a brightness ramp; drawing in ones over a zero background, they multiply a row of packed 4-bit pixels by a single constant to apply a 1-3-1 convolution kernel, spreading each pixel to its neighbours in one operation, processes rows with above, current and below buffers, pokes them back into screen memory, and remaps the palette to a gradient ([Greg L 2026, 22:36](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=1356)).

### Display that reacts and moves

Younès Rabii's Pokemon Glitch makes corruption part of the game rather than a skin: walls change colour organically when you interact with items, forests become extra creepy, and wrong turns lead to "dimensions" with infinite staircases ([Younès Rabii 2021, 3:39](https://youtu.be/Ove6z8zDsjE?t=219)). Ben Berman, arguing in 2017 that more accessible roguelikes require thinking critically about art, showed neural-network character animation trained on about 30 hours of motion capture: movement of film quality generated from controller input alone, climbing stairs and running into walls on a heightmap terrain, which Berman said could be used in a game then ([Ben Berman 2017, 10:17](https://youtu.be/Z6lHExfem6U?t=617)).

### Off the screen

Some generators leave the display entirely. bleeptrack turned a flower generator into printed fabric by arranging many outputs as a texture with a fixed palette, each flower unique but the colours constant, and suggests that if your generator makes single objects you can arrange its outputs into a texture ([bleeptrack 2025, 8:29](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=509)). With a laser cutter at reduced power bleeptrack engraves as well as cuts paper, layering dark and colourful sheets into about 200 generated beetle patches, and cuts generated snowflakes, while stressing the considerable manual work involved ([bleeptrack 2025, 16:56](https://youtu.be/FWQwtn-46rs?t=1016)). Nat Alison's visualisations of primes and coprimes, a "modular mandala" and "prime logs", show patterns that repeat clearly strand by strand yet are hard to predict globally, then line up unexpectedly, a picture of the balance between local order and global chaos that procedural designers chase ([Nat Alison 2024, 14:55](https://youtu.be/5_UET-rUtGU?t=895)).

**In practice:** treat the display (grid, palette, renderer, even the physical medium) as something you can still explore rather than a solved problem. None of these is established roguelike practice; they are open directions, and Montfort could not name a roguelike that meets the challenge.

## Tensions and open questions

**Store-bought assets: casting call or stock photo?** Sergio Garces treats store assets as a legitimate starting point, like casting an actor rather than inventing one, and unifies them by replacing materials and buying within one style ([Sergio Garces 2022, 4:02](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=242); [Sergio Garces 2022, 8:42](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=522)). Sofie Kjær Schmidt uses them for testing and speed but warns that they come without source files and can make a game look like a series of stock photos, and relies on post-processing to pull them together ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048)). The choice depends on how much unifying work you can afford and how distinctive your look needs to be.

**Does abstraction make players imagine on its own?** droqen and Jamie Brittain argue that low fidelity invites players to fill in the world and co-create it ([droqen 2020, 9:01](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=541); [Jamie Brittain 2026, 17:12](https://youtu.be/C2CzHLtt1Fw?t=1032)). Evan Ovadia found that switching to ASCII is only a first step: imagination needs a small trigger of detail, too much colour and detail can stop it, and Ovadia calls the secret an open question ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364)). Nobody in the talks says how much detail is the right amount.

**Graphics, half-measures and middle paths.** Santiago Zapata and Thomas Biskup agree that reaching a mainstream audience means graphics ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 16:42](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1002)), and Zapata warns that replacing each character with a static sprite is a half-measure that satisfies nobody: go all the way or stay with characters ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977)). Josh Ge suggests other ways to keep the roguelike look while reaching more players: animated interfaces, which Ge says attract mainstream audiences, and, since most players use tiles, monochrome tiles that read like glyphs ([Josh Ge 2016, 25:57](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1557); [Josh Ge 2016, 23:54](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1434)). Whether Ge's middle path is the half-measure Zapata warns against, or a different thing, depends on whether it reads as a deliberate style; the talks do not settle it. Ovadia sees their own ASCII-sprite hybrid as one of many combinations still to be found ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 8:54](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=534)).

**How much should juice say?** Juice has a tone, and Jeremiah Reid notes that bouncy effects that suit a silly game might not suit a game like Infra Arcana at all ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:00](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1620)). Tabea Iseli found that almost half the standard screenshake techniques assume violence, so a non-violent game has to build its own feel from scratch ([Tabea Iseli 2022, 10:34](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=634)). And whether heavy juice can sit on a deep classic roguelike without costing depth is unanswered: Chris McCormick would like to see someone try it ([Chris McCormick 2021, 30:28](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1828)).

**Curate or trust the dice?** Paul Hembree says a single generative rule is never enough and the composer must curate and layer ([Paul Hembree 2026, 19:46](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1186)). Sonat Uzun mostly trusts randomness, steering only with scales and silences ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 28:45](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1725)). As the generative music section suggests, the amount of curation you need may depend on how tightly the representation already constrains the output; that is this chapter's reading, not a claim either speaker made.

**The unanswered challenge.** Nick Montfort asks for a roguelike that does with the computer display what Steve McCaffery's Carnival did with the typewriter, and could not name one that already does ([Nick Montfort 2016, 16:37](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=997)).

## Checklist

- Does your content plan (cast size, interactions) fit the representation you chose, and have you costed graphics for every item, monster and interaction? ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 15:24](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=924); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 31:49](https://youtu.be/5CQP8ndTjEY?t=1909))
- Who is your audience, and does your art meet the standard they expect, or is it a half-measure? ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 15:49](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=949); [Santiago Zapata 2018, 16:17](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=977))
- Where does your presentation leave room for the player's imagination, and what small detail triggers it? ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 6:04](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=364))
- If you borrow a retro look, what story does that old medium tell? ([Cara Esten Hurtle 2022, 15:15](https://youtu.be/ua2Brr6KCJM?t=915))
- Have you chosen your character set and palette, or your tile palette, as deliberately as a font? ([JP LeBreton 2019, 10:22](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=622); [Jeremiah Reid 2021, 13:55](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=835); [Joel Ryan 2022, 11:20](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=680))
- Can an experienced player identify every tile by its major forms and silhouette, and does size signal threat? ([Joel Ryan 2022, 24:02](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=1442); [Joel Ryan 2022, 15:08](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=908); [Joel Ryan 2022, 15:58](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=958))
- Does each creature's look teach what it does, and does its visible state reflect what your systems track? ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 26:16](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1576); [Liza Knipscher 2025, 5:06](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=306))
- Are your assets from one coherent style, with materials and post-processing that make them agree? ([Sergio Garces 2022, 6:30](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=390); [Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 17:28](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1048))
- Do your generated spaces have focal points, grounded props and enough contrast in detail for the eye to rest? ([Max Bottega 2024, 9:08](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=548); [Max Bottega 2024, 7:18](https://youtu.be/27gUUW20fn8?t=438); [Loren Schmidt 2024, 30:58](https://youtu.be/FaLUhh_Vfmk?t=1858))
- Does every turn produce visible, non-blocking feedback that fits the game's tone and verbs? ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:00](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1620); [Tabea Iseli 2022, 10:34](https://youtu.be/ZJAgY73c8bA?t=634))
- What does each feedback sound say about the act it confirms? ([Xalavier Nelson Jr. 2021, 17:00](https://youtu.be/SdQxLThAbs8?t=1020))
- Would you listen to each track for 15 minutes outside the game, and can a player tell where in the loop they are? ([Crashtroid 2023, 15:01](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=901); [Crashtroid 2023, 3:46](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=226))
- Do changes in music mark the player's progress, and does the music follow a game variable rather than a fixed timeline? ([Crashtroid 2023, 13:43](https://youtu.be/avVsu4VLhes?t=823); [Paul Hembree 2023, 3:55](https://youtu.be/S5Ukp6AOdQY?t=235))
- If you generate music, what representation constrains it, and where does a human curate the output? ([Paul Hembree 2026, 19:46](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1186); [Paul Hembree 2026, 29:34](https://youtu.be/DJqBTJioVqM?t=1774))
